summary:
Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, and Nunavut stands under that national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal identity documents can carry an X marker, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and no jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Nunavut layers its own statutory protection on top of that federal floor. In March 2017 Nunavut MLAs voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31, amending the territory's Human Rights Act to add gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation as protected grounds. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At that point nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws, which made Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

Nunavut's Vital Statistics Act now carries a third sex designation on birth certificates. On 18 September 2025 MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore the non-binary option after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill; the bill then passed third reading. Sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government also funds transition-related care. From March 2022 Nunavut's Health Department funded breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty for transgender and non-binary residents under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the step overdue while flagging information gaps for residents outside the capital.

National hate-crime data sets the surrounding risk picture. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024', published 30 March 2026, records 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents, up 1% over the year and 169% since 2018, a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and 184% above 2020. Sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50. Rates run roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a gap that matters for a territory with no metropolitan reporting hub.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report works through police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations and supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.
tangentialFactors:
The correctional system is the weakest point in the Canadian record. Federal policy after Bill C-16 holds that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners and elevated risk of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These conditions bear on a visitor only if detained.

Sub-provincial policy turbulence elsewhere in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport and falls mainly on minors and residents. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act used the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or their gender identity at school, drawing repeal calls and litigation. Alberta passed health, education and sport statutes in 2024 and shielded them through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again invoking the notwithstanding clause.

The pace of change in Nunavut contrasts with the 2017 baseline, when only nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws; the territory now sits with the rest of Canada on non-binary recognition as well as on protected grounds.

The national statistics show divergent directions within the same year: gender identity and expression motivations climbed for a fourth consecutive year while sexual-orientation motivations fell, so an aggregate decline in hate crime does not describe the trans-specific trend.
localsOnly:
Residents of Nunavut may rely on the territorial Human Rights Act as amended by Bill 31, which lists gender identity and gender expression as protected grounds alongside sexual orientation, in addition to the federal Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code hate-motivation provisions.

Residents can request a non-binary sex designation on a Nunavut birth certificate under the Vital Statistics Act as amended in September 2025, a change the bill's sponsor framed as bringing the territory into line with the rest of Canada.

Transition-related care is funded by Nunavut's Health Department for transgender and non-binary residents under the arrangement with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal, covering breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty. Positive Space has noted that residents outside the capital face gaps in information about accessing that care.

Police-reported hate-crime statistics nationally break out gender identity or expression as a motivation category, giving residents a documented basis for tracking incidents of this kind, though the annual release is national in scope.
outOfScopeNotes:
Territory-level hate-crime counts for Nunavut are unresolved: the Statistics Canada release reports national totals and metropolitan-versus-smaller-town rate differentials, and this inventory does not establish a Nunavut figure or a territorial breakdown.

The enforcement record for Nunavut's Human Rights Act amendments, including any complaint filed on grounds of gender identity or expression and its outcome, is not sourced here.

Whether the non-binary designation introduced on Nunavut birth certificates extends to the territorial driver's licence, health card or other identity documents is not sourced in this inventory; the X marker referenced for federal documents is a separate instrument.

The practical availability of transition-related care to a short-term visitor, as distinct from a resident, is not addressed by the sources; the funded programme is described as serving transgender and non-binary residents.

Egale Canada's analysis is national in scope and no territorial equivalent from Nunavut is cited, so local victimisation levels remain unquantified.
